App Review rejected iOS 0.5.0 (build 37) **twice on the same submission**
`2b27f1e4-9f5e-4f50-803e-f14fe3ca48dc`. macOS 0.5.0 was approved from the same code on 2026-08-29
(submission `41b10c68`), so both demands belong to the iOS reviewer, not to the account.

**Round 1, 2026-09-01 — Guideline 2.1.** They asked for a demo video of the current build on a physical
device, with the initial pairing and the whole workflow. `docs/media/demo.mp4` answered it, linked from the
review notes.

**Round 2, 2026-09-03 — Guideline 2.1(a).** The reviewer ran the build on an iPad Pro 11-inch (M4), selected
the "HF" segment on the Connect screen, met the huggingface.co login page and stopped. The letter says
outright that **a demo video is not sufficient** — so round 1's answer does not carry over. The formal
trigger was `demoAccountRequired: false` in App Review Information beside a live sign-in screen: any way in
that asks for credentials needs credentials in that section, whatever else the notes offer.

**Why the simulator did not cover it:** the notes already pointed at `ConnectRoute.simulator` and the reviewer
read them. A demonstration mode answers "show us the features"; it does not answer "let us in". Both halves
of 2.1(a) need their own answer — credentials for the account, the simulator for pre-populated content.

**How it was closed (2026-09-04, no new build):** a throwaway Hugging Face account
(`alexey1312ru+hfreview@gmail.com`, no 2FA, plus-alias because HF refuses a second account on one address),
`demoAccountRequired: true`, and notes rewritten to open with the account rather than with the simulator.
The account has **no robot linked**, so "Your Reachies" shows `No Reachy online` — the notes name that screen
as the correct result, which turns an empty list from "we could not verify" into the proof that nothing else
hides behind the sign-in.

**Sharing the real robot was refused and stays refused.** A robot linked to a demo account gives a stranger
its camera and microphone in a private home, for an unpredictable multi-day review window. Do not offer it.

**Held in reserve for a third round:** the approved macOS build of the same source, as the control that the
app is reviewable and the account is healthy.

**Update Review re-stamps the submission.** `submittedDate` on `2b27f1e4` moved to 2026-09-04T17:52Z and the
state went to `WAITING_FOR_REVIEW` — same submission id, same build. Save the review notes **before** replying
in the Resolution Center and before pressing the button, or the reviewer comes back to the old ones.
The rejection text itself is only in the Resolution Center: the API reports `REJECTED` / `UNRESOLVED_ISSUES`
with no message. See [[review-notes-live-only-in-asc]] and [[app-store-submission-gates]].
== review-notes ==
---
name: review-notes-live-only-in-asc
description: App Review and Beta App Review notes live only on the server, so they silently fall behind the build; editing them does not reset the review queue
metadata:
  type: project
---

App Review notes, Beta App Review notes and the TestFlight page description are
stored only in App Store Connect — nothing in this repository holds them, so no
diff and no CI job can catch them going stale. On 2026-08-31 all three still said
"HARDWARE REQUIRED … There is no demo mode, no mock data and no test account" and
named the Connect screen's third segment "Manual", while 0.5.0 had shipped
`ConnectRoute.simulator` and the App Store description already advertised
"TRY IT WITHOUT A ROBOT". The reviewer was reading that the app could not be
evaluated at all.

**Why:** a reviewer who cannot exercise the app is the usual cause of a long
Waiting for Review and of a Guideline 2.1 rejection. macOS 0.5.0 cleared review in
hours on 2026-08-29; iOS, submitted four minutes later, was still queued two days
on.

**How to apply:** re-read the notes against the build whenever a release adds a way
in that needs no robot. `asc review details-for-version --version-id …` for App
Review, `asc testflight review view --app …` for the beta pair. Editing notes with
`review details-update` while the version sits in WAITING_FOR_REVIEW is safe — the
state and `submittedDate` on the reviewSubmission both stayed put, so the queue
position is not lost. Replacing the build would reset it. Also note that
`versions list` prints the version record's `createdDate`, which reads as a much
older submission than the real one — the date that matters is
`submittedDate` on `review submissions-list`. See [[app-store-submission-gates]]
and [[asc-review-submit-manual-finish]].
== testflight-highest ==
---
name: testflight-picks-highest-build-number
description: TestFlight shows the build with the highest CFBundleVersion, not the newest upload, so a lower build number hides a newer version
metadata:
  type: project
---

TestFlight offers testers the build with the **highest CFBundleVersion**, not the
most recent upload and not the highest marketing version. On 2026-09-01 iOS 0.5.0
was build 40 while 0.4.2 was build 177, so the public TestFlight page kept showing
0.4.2 — although build 40 was VALID, BETA_APPROVED and in the Public Beta group.
macOS was correct at the same moment (0.5.0 = build 180 > 177).

App Store Connect does not catch this: it only demands a rising CFBundleVersion
**inside one marketing version on one platform**, so 40 was accepted after 39.

The iOS 0.5.0 builds are 37, 38, 39, 40 — Xcode Cloud's own counter, not the
`COMMIT_COUNT + CI_BUILD_NUMBER` that `Apps/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` stamps
(that would give ~226, and the script fails loudly if its sed matches nothing or
the count is at or below BUILD_NUMBER_FLOOR=150). So the number the script writes
does not reach the artifact — suspect "Xcode Cloud manages build numbers" in App
Store Connect. Read `Archiving build N` in the Xcode Cloud log to confirm.

**Why:** a green upload and an approved beta review still leave testers on the old
version, and nothing in the API reports it as a problem.

**How to apply:** compare build numbers across marketing versions, not dates, when
TestFlight looks stale. Fix by uploading a local release ([[verify-testflight-upload]]),
whose number is `git rev-list --count HEAD` and therefore above every Xcode Cloud one.
== ios waits ==
---
name: ios-0-4-0-waits-on-0-3-0-review
description: iOS is deliberately not submitted to the App Store — it waits for the verdict on 0.3.0, in review since 2026-08-17; only TestFlight ships on iOS
metadata:
  type: project
---

On 2026-08-19 macOS **0.4.1** went to review (version `c7f715a4-a340-4a1c-bf7c-820d67b509b5`,
build 164) while **iOS was left unsubmitted on purpose**. iOS 0.3.0 has been in
`WAITING_FOR_REVIEW` since 2026-08-17 and App Store Connect refuses a second version in
review, so submitting iOS would mean cancelling 0.3.0 and losing its place in the queue.
Both platforms carry build 164 on TestFlight.

**Why:** iOS has never been approved, so 0.3.0's verdict decides two things at once — the
first live iOS version, and whether `whatsNew` is accepted on iOS at all.

**How to apply:** check `asc versions list --app 6799644194` first. Once 0.3.0 resolves,
submit iOS the same way macOS went: `versions create --platform IOS`, `metadata push`
(drop `whatsNew` if iOS is still unapproved), `review details-update` with the simulator
notes, then the manual submission finish in [[asc-review-submit-manual-finish]].
While 0.3.0 sits in review the app carries two app infos, so `asc validate` cannot answer
at all — check age rating and screenshots by hand. See [[app-store-submission-gates]].
== rename version ==
---
name: rename-version-instead-of-creating-one
description: A withdrawn App Store version is renamed with `versions update --version`, which keeps review details, screenshots and localizations that a new version would lose
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

To re-release a version that was pulled out of review, **rename it** rather than create a
new one: `asc submit cancel --id <submission>` leaves the version in `DEVELOPER_REJECTED`,
which is editable, and `asc versions update --version-id <id> --version 0.4.1` moves it to
the new number. Measured on 2026-08-19 for macOS 0.4.0 → 0.4.1: the App Review Information
(contacts and the `com.apple.security.network.server` justification), all six screenshots
and the version localization survived untouched. Only the attached build detaches.

**Why:** App Review Information is per version and per platform, lives only on the server,
and is absent from `metadata/`. A fresh `versions create` starts empty and every one of
those records has to be written again.

**How to apply:** cancel → `versions update --version` → `metadata push` for the changed
fields → `versions attach-build` → submit. Verify the notes survived with
`asc review details-for-version --version-id <id>` before submitting.
See [[asc-review-submit-manual-finish]].
== manual finish ==
---
name: asc-review-submit-manual-finish
description: `asc review submit` needs --build and dies on a request timeout, leaving an empty draft; finish it with items-add --item-type appStoreVersions and submissions-submit
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`asc review submit` failed twice on 2026-08-19 (asc 3.7.0) before macOS 0.4.1 reached review:

1. Without `--build <build-id>` it exits on `Error: --build is required`, even when the
   build is already attached to the version.
2. With it, the `POST /v1/reviewSubmissionItems` call hit `context deadline exceeded` and
   preserved an **empty** draft submission.

Finish that draft by hand — the item type is not obvious:

```bash
export ASC_TIMEOUT=120s
asc review items-list --submission <sub>                                    # confirm it is empty
asc review items-add --submission <sub> --item-type appStoreVersions --item-id <version-id>
asc review submissions-submit --id <sub> --confirm
asc versions list --app 6799644194                                          # WAITING_FOR_REVIEW
```

**Why:** the wrapper's three inner calls are each retryable, but a half-run leaves a draft
that later reads as stale. Reusing it costs nothing and avoids that.

**How to apply:** read the outcome off the version state, never off the exit code — which is
the same rule the false-negative documented in `docs/release.md` needs.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains

   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

Это разобрано, и не в этой сессии — 27 августа по sysdiagnose с iPhone 17 Pro. Оно записано в память как измеренный факт, а не догадка:

Система рисует third-party LiveCommunicationKit звонок **только** компактной пилюлей — `SBSystemApertureStatusBarPillElement`, `preferredLayoutMode: compact` на всю жизнь звонка, **никогда** `expanded`. Владелец элемента — SpringBoard, `layoutModeChangeReason: client`: решает система, не приложение. API, чтобы раскрыть её, не существует. Строк показа на lock screen — ноль.

При этом сам звонок здоров: `callservicesd` пишет `stat=Active`, `providerName Hey Reachy`, состояния `Sending → Active → Disconnected` приходят все. Приложение сообщает системе всё правильно — «нераскрывающаяся пилюля» это и есть весь системный UI, который iOS даёт не-FaceTime звонку.

★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────
И вот почему её не видно на твоём видео: пока приложение на переднем плане, пилюля подавлена принудительно — `associatedBundleIdentifiersToSuppressInSystemAperture: (com.alexey1312.ReachyMini)`. Чтобы её снять, нужно **свернуть приложение** свайпом домой. Тогда она появится рядом с часами.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Значит сценарий меняется — пункты про mute и End «из системного UI» вычёркиваем, их физически нет:

1. Live → тап по микрофону → разрешение → **Allow**
2. **Свайп домой** — на домашнем экране видна пилюля звонка рядом с часами (вот он, системный UI)
3. Вернуться в приложение — mute/unmute кнопкой микрофона
4. **«End call»** красной кнопкой в приложении
5. Phone → Recents: строка `reachy_mini`, тап по ней — приложение открывается и звонок стартует снова (redial)

CALL SERVICES - WHAT THE APP USES

The app carries two-way voice with the robot. The user speaks, the robot plays
the voice through its speaker, and the robot's microphone comes back. The app
presents that session as a system call through LiveCommunicationKit, which is
the successor to CallKit.

The app starts calls. It never receives them. A call always goes out to a robot
that the user owns. No other person can call this app, so the app registers no
VoIP push and never reports an incoming call. The "voip" background mode is what
entitles ConversationManager to perform a call transaction. Without that mode
the framework refuses the transaction.

- Start a call, from the microphone button.
- Mute and unmute during a call.
- End a call, from the red button in the app.
- Donate the call to Recents, so the Phone app can call the robot again.

iOS gives a call from an app other than FaceTime one compact pill beside the
clock. The pill does not expand and it carries no buttons. iOS also hides the
pill while the app is in the foreground. So the video puts the app in the
background to show it. The user ends the call in the app, because the system
shows no End button for such a call.

linked to that account. The sign-in is optional. All other functions work

3. The app builds a robot from its own description and opens the main tabs.

The simulator answers the Live tab, the Robot tab and Settings. It declines the
camera, the two-way audio, the app catalogue, the moves, the soundboard and the
Wi-Fi setup. Each one belongs to a physical machine.

FIRST LAUNCH

A Bluetooth sheet opens over the Connect screen at the first launch. Dismiss it
with Cancel. The iOS Local Network alert waits below it. Allow it, or select the
"Simulator" segment, which needs no permission.

#!/bin/sh
# =============================================================================
# Keep SwiftPM off a beta Xcode's SDK — sourced, never executed
# =============================================================================
# The swift.org toolchain pinned in `.swift-version` cannot read every SDK a beta
# Xcode ships. Swift 6.3.0 against Xcode 27 beta's macOS 27 SDK puts the backing
# storage of a `@State private` property into the synthesised memberwise
# initialiser, which makes that initialiser private too. ReachyUI then refuses to
# compile at 401 call sites across ten types — this line first said thirteen, which
# was the count before anyone re-measured it (`docs/research/ios-27.md`):
#
#     error: 'LogConsoleView' initializer is inaccessible due to
#     'private' protection level
#
# The same source builds green under Xcode 27's own Swift 6.4 and on CI, whose
# `lint-test` job runs SwiftPM on an image with a release SDK. So this is the SDK,
# not the code, and the machine already carries a release SDK beside the beta one:
# the Command Line Tools ship theirs at a path of their own.
#
# Only while a beta Xcode is selected. The override removes itself the day the
# release arrives, and it does nothing on Linux, where `xcode-select` is absent.
# Case-folded: Apple ships `Xcode-beta.app` and Xcodes.app names the same build
# `Xcode-27.0.0-Beta.6.app`, so matching one spelling silently misses the other.
#
# **And only for a swift.org toolchain, which is what the paragraph above is about.**
# Xcode's own Swift reads the beta SDK perfectly well — `swift build` against Xcode 27
# beta 6's macOS 27 SDK completes in 32 s here, the same configuration `lint-test`
# builds in — so swapping the SDK out from under a machine with no swiftly installed
# bought nothing and cost the one thing #124 needed: a `Sources/` that names an iOS 27
# symbol cannot compile against a 26.5 SDK, so every local `mise run build` and
# `mise run test` would fail over declarations the four app jobs build happily.
#
# A swift.org toolchain keeps the swap, and now for a second reason as well as the
# first: it cannot build this package against either SDK any more — 27 symbols are
# absent from 26.5 — and "cannot find 'LongRunningIntent' in scope" is a far better
# thing to read than 401 inaccessible-initialiser errors across ten types.
#
# The version line is the measurement rather than a path guess: Xcode's toolchain
# stamps `swiftlang-6.4.0.33.1`, a swift.org build stamps `swift-6.3.3-RELEASE`.

*beta*)

		export SDKROOT
	fi
	;;
